utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, everyone. Madam Registrar, please call the case that is listed on the docket for today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, good afternoon. This is case number IT-95-17-A, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Bralo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. I would like to see whether Mr. Bralo can hear and follow the proceedings in a language that he understands. The Appellant BRALO: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am now going to move to the appearances, starting with the representatives of the office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Madam President, Your Honours, Peter Kremer appearing on behalf of the Prosecution with Xavier Tracol and Kristina Carey. Our case manager, Lourdes Galicia, is with us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kremer. Now I am going to turn to the Defence. May I have the appearances please for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, Madam President. My name is Jonathan Cooper; I appear as lead counsel, together with Virginia Lindsay, my co-counsel. We are joined by Ms. Grgic [phoen], who is our interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cooper. The Appeals Chamber is sitting today to hear the submissions of the parties with respect to the appeal filed by Mr. Bralo against the Sentencing Judgement. I will summarise the grounds of appeal raised before the Appeals Chamber and I will explain how we will proceed this afternoon. Miroslav Bralo appealed the Trial Judgement that was delivered on the 7th of December, 2005, by Trial Chamber III that was made up of Judges Bonomy, who was the Presiding Judge, Judge Robinson, and Judge Kwon. A spot of the Trial Judgement. The Trial Chamber sentenced Miroslav Bralo to 20 years' imprisonment after having accepted his guilty pleas on the 19th of July, 2005, pleas entered against eight counts he was charged with. And more specifically, these counts were a count of persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, under Articles 5 (h) and 7.1 of the Statute of the Tribunal. Four counts of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, including acts of torture or inhuman treatment, unlawful confinement punishable under Articles 2 (b), 2 (g), and 7.1 of the Statute. Three counts of violation of the laws and customs of war, punishable under Articles 3 and 7.1 of the Statute, including murder, torture, and outrages upon personal dignity, including rape. Mr. Bralo appealed against the Sentencing Judgement on the 5th of January, 2006. He filed his brief on appeal on the 30th of March, 2006. In his brief the Appellant generally submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law and abused its discretion when passing a sentence which was excessive. He submits that the sentence that was imposed upon him occasioned a miscarriage of justice because the sentence does not properly reflect substantial mitigating circumstances in this case. In support of his argument, he specifically submits that, first of all, the Trial Chamber erred when assessing some matters as wholly irrelevant to sentence, and when finding that they could not be considered in mitigation. Secondly, that the Trial Chamber did not ascribe sufficient weight to the factors it accepted as relevant. And finally, that the Trial Chamber should have imposed a lesser sentence, considering the volume and the quality of mitigating circumstances. Under his first ground of appeal, the Appellant submits that while the Trial Chamber did consider his submissions, it did not hold that the following factors were to be taken into account in mitigation. First of all, the deteriorating military and political situation in the Lasva Valley in 1992 and 1993. Secondly, the attack on the Appellant and his wife at their home in February 1993. Thirdly, the fact that the Appellant was released from prison on condition that he participates in the attack on the village of Ahmici. Fourthly, the manner in which he was used by his superiors. Under his second ground of appeal the Appellant contends that the Trial Chamber, has erred when it failed to attach proper weight to his personal circumstances and to his positive cooperation of value to the Prosecutor, the Tribunal, and the people of Ahmici. He submits among other things that the cooperation he provided to the Prosecution was substantial within the meaning of Rule 101 (B) (ii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, whereas the Trial Chamber simply qualified that cooperation as moderate and described that it was merely that there was a mere willingness on his part to give information. Finally, the Appellant submits that the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber both acknowledge that his guilty plea was based on genuine remorse, remorse that he expressed publicly. The Appellant contends in this respect that the expression of genuine remorse that goes beyond the mere fact of acknowledging his crimes by pleading guilty, is one of the most significant and important mitigating circumstances. He stresses, furthermore, that his behaviour after the conflict demonstrates the efforts he made to express his remorse, whereas the sentence that was passed upon him does not fully reflect these acts, these efforts, that contributed to restoring the peace in the region. Under his third ground of appeal the Appellant argues that the Trial Chamber, after it determined that the mitigating evidence, together warranted substantial modification of the sentence, abused its discretion when reducing the sentence only by five years. Finally, I would like to recall that on the 12th of January, 2007, the Appeals Chamber admitted three additional exhibits under Rule 115 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We have also received two supplemental briefs from the Appellant in support of his second and his third grounds of appeal. In his first supplemental brief the Appellant argues in support of that ground of appeal, the ground of appeal dealing with the cooperation he provided to the Prosecution, the Appellant states that the Prosecutor used the factual basis that was part and parcel of the plea agreement during the review proceedings in the Blaskic case. In his second supplemental brief, the Appellant develops his arguments with respect firstly to what he meant by the error, the alleged error of the Trial Chamber regarding the standard of proof that was applied by the Trial Chamber when assessing the level of cooperation of the Appellant with the Prosecution. And secondly, this is in relation to the alleged error committed by the Trial Chamber who -- which allegedly failed to properly consider the issue of cooperation. The Appellant therefore requests the Appeals Chamber to reconsider and to reduce his sentence in light of these alleged errors that, according to him, invalidates the Sentencing Judgement. The Prosecution requests the Appeals Chamber to dismiss all grounds of appeal submitted by the Appellant. During today's hearing the parties are free to decide in what way they want to make their submissions about their grounds of appeal. However, I would like to remind the Prosecution and the Defence of Mr. Bralo that they were invited to elaborate on a number of points that were listed in the scheduling order of 10th of January 2007, and I'm not going to repeat what was contained in the scheduling order. However, I would like now to recall what is the standard for appellate review for alleged factual and legal errors. Sentencing appeals, as appeals from any Judgement, are appeals strictu sensu they are of a corrective nature and they are not trials de novo. The Appellant therefore, cannot merely repeat the arguments made at trial. Pursuant to Article 25 of the Statute, the role of the Appeals Chamber is limited to correcting errors of law, invalidating a decision, and errors of fact which have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. Therefore, as a general rule, the Appeals Chamber will not revise a sentence unless the Trial Chamber has committed a discernible error in exercising its discretion or has failed to follow the applicable law. It is for the Appellant to demonstrate how the Trial Chamber abused its discretion in imposing his sentence. The Appellant is furthermore under the obligation to provide specific references to the elements used in support of his submissions on appeal. The hearing of today will be organised according to what was stated in the scheduling order of 10th of January 2007. We will first hear the submissions of the Defence; the Defence will have one hour and a half to do so. After that we will have a 20-minute break, and the Prosecution will then make its submissions in response to the Defence, and the Prosecution will have one hour to do so. Then the Defence will have 45 minutes to reply to the Prosecution's submissions. Finally, Mr. Bralo will be invited to take the floor, if he wishes to do so, for a short statement that should not exceed 15 minutes. The Appeals Chamber would find it extremely useful if the parties were able to submit and present their arguments in a clear, concise, and well-organised manner. At any time during the proceedings the Judges will feel free to interrupt the parties to request specifications or ask questions, questions that will also possibly be put at the end of each presentation. If there aren't any questions related to the way we shall proceed this afternoon, I would now like to invite the Defence to make its submissions. Mr. Cooper, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Madam President, Your Honours. This case is about mitigation, about the legal obligations conferred by Article 24, and Rule 101, upon a Trial Chamber to consider individual elements in mitigation, to give appropriate weight to individual factors in mitigation, and to ensure that the mitigation is translated over all into an appropriate reduction of sentence. In the light of your admission of fresh evidence under Rule 115, a further issue arises as to the appropriate standard of review when an Appeals Chamber hears a sentence appeal in a fresh-evidence case, and what consequences may flow from the admission of fresh evidence. Madam President, we are grateful for your introduction to this appeal hearing. We are confident that Your Honours are familiar with the pleadings. Our oral submissions are intended to highlight key areas already referred to in the pleadings, and to address in full the questions that Your Honours may have. We intend to divide our time into two. In a moment I'll give the floor to Ms. Lindsay to deal with the first of our three subgrounds of appeal. We then propose to split the second one down the middle between us, and I will deal with the third. At the conclusion of all our oral arguments in this case, we envisage completing the proceedings with a short statement from the Appellant. So before handing over to Ms. Lindsay, we thought it helpful if I addressed straight away the issue of the standard of review, in the light of the new evidence that has been admitted. Plainly the grounds of appeal were drafted back on the 5th of January, 2006, and, as Your Honours know, in the 13 months since grounds were drafted, there has been a great deal of activity in this case relating to disclosure of information. It has now emerged that the Appellant did not receive, at the sentencing stage, all the material he was entitled to receive under Rule 68. We are assured that this defect has now been addressed by the Prosecution, and the result has been service of a number of elements of further material which have been reflected firstly in the supplemental brief, as Your Honour noted. That addressed material which was known to the Trial Chamber at the time of sentence, but not to the Defendant. The second supplemental brief included some Rule 68 material and some further material which has arisen some before and some since the date of sentence. Now, none of that material was known either to the Defendant, this Appellant, or to the Trial Chamber. In the latter case the material was admitted because in your words, Madam President, it could have been a decisive factor in weighing Mr. Bralo's cooperation and could have changed the sentence. Now, what are the consequences of admission in terms of the procedure to be adopted and the standard of review to apply? This is a matter which is addressed in the Prosecution reply to the second supplemental brief, and Your Honours know that that was filed two days ago on the 7th of February, and we intend to reply to it, both in this oral argument and, if necessary, in a short reply in due course. With respect to the Prosecution, we agree with their initial conclusions regarding the standard of review which now must apply in this case. We say that with the caveat that because of the legal and procedural and factual errors that have been raised, the first instance review referred to by the Prosecution is limited first to the record before the Trial Chamber, and then when and if it becomes necessary to the additional evidence. The first question is a need for a review of sentence. The parties, Your Honours, agree that consideration of mitigating circumstances can never be made in isolation from the gravity of the offence and the aggravating circumstances, and it follows that the effect of the admission of the new material, whoever may have been to blame for it not being before the Court, is that the sentence exercise should proceed on the basis of a full evaluation of the totality of the evidence adduced at the sentence stage and admitted pursuant to Rule 115. Secondly, is there a need for a complete rehearing? We submit not. We submit there is no need for a rehearing de novo, nor that the Trial Chamber's efforts in this case are rendered a nullity because of the failure to disclose to them information that was necessary for a proper sentence. The situation appears to be similar to that in the Celebici case, where what was required following a number of acquittals in the Appeals Chamber was resolution of the issue of whether any adjustment should made to the sentences because of the matters referred to and not a complete rehearing on the issue of sentence. It begs a third question. Which should be the Chamber to conduct such a sentencing exercise? We submit that the only proper course is to remit this matter to the original Trial Chamber for reconsideration of sentence in the light of this new material. Were it otherwise, the Appeals Chamber would be asked to assess the evidence afresh and to pass a sentence from which there could be no effective appeal. It would mean that the Appellant would have but this single chance to make representations to a sentencing Court on the basis of all the material available and relevant to sentence. That would have the effect that this appeal hearing would dissolve into a hearing de novo, a fresh hearing ab initio of the merits of the case. We submit, on the contrary, that the weighing of factual evidence, the forming judgements about it, about relative weight of mitigation and aggravating features, and the initial assessment of appropriate sentence, these are all matters which are preeminently in the province of a first-instance Chamber rather than an Appeal Chamber and from which there should be an effective appeal since Appellant correction is an important element in the right to a fair trial. Once again this Tribunal has the experience of doing exactly that in the Celebici case, and in that that case the matters of Delic, Landzo, and Mucic, were remitted to the Trial Chamber for reconsideration in order that there could be consideration of sentence by a Chamber from which, in the Appeals Chamber's words, an appeal is possible. Now, I'm very conscious that this Appeals Chamber took a different course in the recent case of Galic, and I have well in mind both that decision and also the dissenting Judgement of your brother Judge, President Pocar, who expressed in his dissenting Judgement the need precisely to ensure a right of appeal. We say that the factual position in this case is more favourable for a remittal to a Trial Chamber, and that's because what is needed here is an answer to the question, should there be an adjustment in the light of the new material, given the totality of the evidence. And since the Trial Chamber has already considered almost the totality of the evidence, it seems an efficient way of disposing of this matter in a way which also safeguards a paramount consideration of fairness. So the Prosecution have described in their brief, and I refer to the response brief to the second supplemental brief, they have described the appropriate approach to this case as being one of first instance, and we agree that the appropriate Court to hear a matter of first instance is a Court of first instance and we submit that the case should be remitted to the original Trial Chamber for that purpose. The fourth matter that arises, and that I deal with briefly is this: That being so, what happens to these grounds of appeal? And it's my submission that each of the original issues on appeal remains relevant and is here to be determined. The grounds don't go away, but they have to be seen in a different light, bearing in mind there needs to be this comprehensive review of the material in the light of the fresh evidence which has emerged. Our submission is that those matters should be resolved for the benefit of whichever Trial Chamber will ultimately pass sentence. And again that was precisely the position in Celebici, where the Appeals Chamber set out their opinion that, and I quote, "It's appropriate that the Appeals Chamber consider and resolve the issues raised in the parties' grounds of appeal relating to sentence insofar as they allege the commission of errors in the exercise of discretion or other errors of law by the Trial Chamber so that the new Trial Chamber will then be in a position to consider what, if any adjustment should be made to the Appeals Chamber -- made to what the Appeals Chamber considers would otherwise have been appropriate sentences." Madam President, Your Honours, that's the position we take in relation to standard of review in these proceedings. Having set out our position on that preliminary point, I give the floor to Ms. Lindsay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Madam President, Your Honours. I will begin with the first subground of our appeal which is that the Trial Chamber erred in assessing certain matters as wholly irrelevant to sentence. Now, as we all know, the Trial Chamber is bound as a matter of law to take into account matters which are relevant to sentence. The failure to do so is discernible error, will require a revision of sentence. In our opening brief, we raised four instances that were read out just a minute ago where the Trial Chamber excluded as irrelevant evidence of mitigating circumstances. And very briefly, again, these are the deteriorating political and military situation in Lasva Valley, the attack on the Appellant and his wife in their own home in February 1993, the first one was also in 1992 and 1993. I'm sorry. The third one is the fact that the Appellant was released from prison on condition that he participate on the attack in Ahmici. And the fourth was the manner in which he was used by his superiors. Now, each of these matters involved clear evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. I believe that Judge Schomburg would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry to interrupt you, counsel. But you just said that the Appellant was released from prison on condition that he participate on the attack in Ahmici, on condition that he participated. Would you and could you elaborate a little bit more what happened to the case of the Prosecution against him as regards this alleged crime at that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: I believe that there's still an indictment in Bosnia. It was -- I guess it was made inactive, and I don't -- I can't tell you what year. But it was in the -- I can find that information out and provide that to you. But it's in the Travnik court for that municipality in Travnik, and an indictment for -- for genocide was filed, and -- but then when he disappeared and many people presumed that he was dead, then it was put into kind of an inactive status, and as far as I know that is still the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, for this alleged crime he was arrested but spent only one or two weeks --

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- in the prison and was sent or was released later on, and nothing happened until now as regards this alleged prior crime?

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: I misunderstood your question, Your Honour, so I confused two different matters. You were asking about the killing of Isad [phoen] Salkic in 1993. I believe those charges were in Zenica court, not Travnik, and I believe that it's -- I don't even know if there was an official putting it into a dormant state or not. I think it's just -- nothing has ever happened with it since he was released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you know exactly how long he spent arrested in -- and then released for the purposes we all know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: I believe it was a little over two months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: And we will return to that heading shortly. Now, each of these four evidences -- or areas of evidence involved clear evidence. Each of them appears to be matters that were accepted by all the parties. Each of these matters was raised in mitigation and was not put forward as a justification; there was no question of material being put forward as a defence to any count in the indictment, regardless of whatever arguments are put forward by the Prosecution, it was never meant in that way. Each of these matters was found to be totally irrelevant by the Trial Chamber. It's not contrary to the what the Prosecution argues. It's not that the Trial Chamber gave it little weight. It decided that these were matters that should not be included in the sentencing considerations, so they were excluded from the sentencing determination. Each of these matters was relevant. They related to Mr. Bralo's unique situation and his role in the crimes that were committed. Now, the Prosecution argues that the gravity of the offence may be sufficient to render mitigating elements irrelevant. We submit that the proper approach is to identify mitigating evidence and then to determine the weight it should receive. Aggravating evidence is relevant to the latter inquiry, but to consider it as part of the initial inquiry would amount to an impermissible double counting of aggravating evidence and the effect -- it would have the effect of depriving Mr. Bralo of any consideration of his individual circumstances. Now, by double counting I mean the material would count once in evaluating the gravity of the offence, and then it would be considered a second time to take away the mitigating -- the mitigation that would otherwise be available. And that's we mean by double counting. Now I will address each of the four areas that were excluded from the sentencing considerations by the Trial Chamber. The first being the deteriorating political and military situation in Lasva Valley in 1992. Now, the Trial Chamber said, and I quote, "The tensions that existed in the region at the relevant time can in no way act in mitigation of the sentence to be imposed upon Bralo." That is an emphatic rejection of the evidence. There is no weight given to it; it wasn't included in the sentencing considerations at all. Both the Prosecution and the Defence presented clear evidence of the breakdown in the political situation, citing previous factual findings of different Trial Chambers in this Tribunal. Three different commanders have been sentenced with this kind of evidence being included in the sentencing considerations. In Celebici, the Trial Chamber sentenced the commander of the Celebici prison camp, and they said, and I quote, "It is relevant and crucial to take into account the circumstances in which the events occurred, as well as the social pressures and hostile environment within which the accused was operating. That's in paragraph 1248. In Aleksovski, the Trial Chamber sentenced the prison warden of Kaonik prison, and said, and I quote, "That crimes took place -- some of the crimes took place while the conflict between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims had reached a peak." Now, the Trial Chamber went on to say that this was not an excuse, but they noted that it was relevant to explaining Aleksovski's role in the crimes committed. In Blaskic the Appeals Chamber sentenced General Blaskic and they found, and I quote again, "The Appeals Chamber sees neither merit nor logic in recognising the mere context of war as a factor to be considered in the mitigation of the criminal conduct of its participants. Nevertheless the Appeals Chamber does consider that the particular circumstances of the Appellant at the outset of and during the war deserve consideration." Now, I would note the personal connection in these cases. If the political situation was relevant for General Blaskic who was Mr. Bralo's commander, and if it was relevant for Mr. Aleksovski, who was Mr. Bralo's prison warden in Kaonik prison then we would submit it is unequal justice for it to be ruled out entirely from consideration in Mr. Bralo's case. Now, the second subheading that I will be addressing in a minute deals with the harm had a was caused by this legal error here, and -- but in that -- under that second heading it is in relation to the Trial Chamber's findings on Mr. Bralo's background and prior character. So I just want to flag that this error, it resulted in evidence being excluded, but then if you look at the evidence of the personal background and character, then you see that also the -- the scope of that evidence was very narrow and we would submit that this is a result of the error under the first ground of appeal. The next area that was excluded entirely was the prior attack with explosives on the Appellant and his wife in their own home in February of 1993. Now, this incident was a crucial point in the evolution of Mr. Bralo. In his -- the path from becoming -- from being a law-abiding citizen of good character to an admitted war criminal. He chased and killed one of three, he believed to have thrown in the middle of the night bombs at his home, at him and his wife, blowing out the windows, bringing down parts of the roof, and making the home uninhabitable. He called the police immediately. He was put in prison, and with the knowledge that he was leaving his wife alone to deal with the house, the neighbours, the relatives of those who threw the bombs and the family of the man who was killed, and there was expert testimony cited by both sides bearing witness to the significance of this type of incident. But once again, we're not raising this as a defence. We're not arguing tu quo. We do not attempt to justify what happened. Yet this evidence was relevant, and it was relevant to show the intense pressures newly brought to bear on Mr. Bralo in February of 1993, and we submit it shows why a short time later Mr. Bralo was targeted by his superiors in April 1993, and why they focused on him to use him as an asset in the -- at Ahmici. They knew he was a soldier who, under attack in a domestic situation, appeared to have snapped only two months earlier and they hoped to exploit that and make it happen again. This provides no excuse. There is no justification for what followed. But we respectfully submit it was error to exclude it from sentencing entirely. We respectfully ask the Appeals Chamber to give consideration for the individual life circumstances in which Mr. Bralo found himself during the time period leading up to the period of the indictment. Now, the third area was excluded as irrelevant was Mr. Bralo's release from prison on condition that he agree to take orders as a member of the Jokers. Again, the material is not in dispute. The evidence shows that, unlike the local that is participated in the attack that day, Mr. Bralo was not a free agent. The Trial Chamber concedes he may have been pressured to participate in the attack, but without evidence of resistance it found the pressure to be irrelevant. The pressure that does not rise to the level of duress may nonetheless be considered as a mitigating circumstances. We know this from Odenovic [phoen], and it is a common holding of many national cases demonstrate this point. On the night of the 15th and 16th of April, 1993, Mr. Bralo was offered his freedom if he agreed to subordinate himself to the Jokers, a new HVO special unit. There was nothing at the time to suggest anything illegal about the offer; it came from his superiors who needed more soldiers. He was told to remain hat prison until after dark because the attack was to be a surprise. When he finally arrived at the Bungalow he found 150 men already there, already having received their orders and ready to participate in the attack. He was given alcohol and told what the orders were, and that was the first time he was alerted that this operation was to be an ethnic cleansing. This is not a justification and it is not an excuse, it does not rise to the level of duress. But its a circumstance that warrants consideration because it shows the unique situation that Mr. Bralo found himself in. The last of the four areas that were excluded as irrelevant is the manner in which the Appellant was used by his superiors. The Trial Chamber said this had no bearing on sentence. The foundation facts are not in issue. The evidence shows he was given alcohol at the prison where he was ordered to wait until after dark, to travel to the Bungalow, and when he arrived at the Bungalow he was given more alcohol and given his orders to kill all, to burn all. The Prosecution's own witnesses -- or witness described how during the months following the attack on the village of Ahmici, Mr. Bralo was used by his superior, Vladimir Santic, to fight with people. The Prosecution argue that being a subordinate to a superior who has intentionally targeted and exploited you is not a mitigating circumstance. I would like to present a hypothetical to illustrate the problem with the Prosecution's position, and I would like to -- in the hypothetical I would say that there is a classroom of 13-year-olds with a teacher and this teacher recruits a group of them to commit burglaries in the neighbourhood. Eventually they're caught, and they're brought to justice. The teacher receives a -- an increased sentence because of the aggravation that arises from the teacher's abuse of its position of trust. At the same time, the students who committed the crimes, when they were sentenced for the crimes they committed, the fact that they were manipulated or influenced, that they were influenced to commit the crimes by someone that they trusted and who was responsible for taking care of them, that's -- that would be a mitigating circumstance for those teenagers. In this case, Mr. Bralo had exhibited an extreme reaction to the attack on his home and had rendered his position vulnerable as a prisoner in a jail, in a town that was threatened to be run over -- overrun by the Bosnian army and was in prison there specifically on account of his own conduct towards a Muslim male, his position could not have been more precarious. Those in authority took advantage of his position and their knowledge of his previous behaviour and they abused their authority, using him as a means towards achievement of their goals. Mr. Harmon noted in his sentencing argument before the Trial Chamber that there is, quote, "There is no doubt that Miroslav Bralo was a useful tool to others." To others with a perverse agenda. The manner in which he was used should have been part of the sentencing considerations. Each of these four areas was relevant to sentence and was erroneously excluded from the sentencing considerations. These are discernible errors and we ask that the evidence be reassessed by an appropriate Chamber and a revised sentence imposed which properly includes this evidence as part of the sentencing consideration. I will now address the second subground which is that the Trial Chamber accepted that personal background and prior character are relevant but erred in assessing the weight to be attached to them. Now, our opening brief raises five matters which were relevant to background and character but that the Trial Chamber failed to consider when assessing Mr. Bralo's personal background and prior character. The Trial Chamber reduced the evidence of his Mr. Bralo's personal background and prior background to two areas: Good character, evidence, and family circumstances. Now, as to good character, they -- in assessing it as having little weight, they presented -- they noted that when crimes are very grave the fact that he may have no history of offending does not necessarily militate in favour of a more lenient sentence. Well, this may be true. But the evidence is nonetheless entitled to some weight, and apparently it was given some weight. Of more concern to this appeal, the evidence considered when making this finding was apparently limited to Mr. Bralo's absence of prior convictions. It appears that the Trial Chamber did not consider his history of overcoming abuse to become a responsible adult. The fact that the war caused him to lose his job in a factory and that -- and then to be drafted -- conscripted into the HVO, and that this was followed by a year of active combat duty fighting the Serbs. The exclusions demonstrate the effect of the legal error in 1.1. The Trial Chamber's standard for relevancy at sentencing was in error, and it led it to first exclude relevant evidence, and now we see the error also distorted the Trial Chamber's analysis of Mr. Bralo's personal background and prior character. The Appeals Chamber in Blaskic at paragraph 15 stated that when they find the application of a wrong legal standard by a Trial Chamber, it is open to the Appeals Chamber to articulate the correct legal standard and to review the relevant findings of the Trial Chamber accordingly. In doing so, the Appeals Chamber not only corrects a legal error, but applies the correct legal standard to the evidence contained in the trial record. And we would submit that that is what is needed to be done in this case, not only with the evidence that was excluded, but with the evidence of good character and the family circumstances. Now, moving on to the family circumstances, the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Bralo was not young and his family circumstances were of minor relevance. And again, the Trial Chamber failed to take into consideration evidence relating to the overall context of the war that impacted upon Mr. Bralo and his family. And I'm just going to focus for this -- for this heading on the location of the family land on the front-line of war. And the Court had a question -- asked that that be clarified. And so I will -- I will try to do that. I can see that in paragraph 7 of the opening brief, we made reference to the proximity of the two houses to each other, but it was not very clear. And I apologise for that. The Bralo family had two houses and they're approximately three and a half kilometres apart. If you see Exhibit B12 there is a witness testimony there, and he estimates that the distance between the Bungalow and Kratine is three and a half to four miles, and the Bungalow is right -- very close to the Bralo house in Nadioci. Mr. Bralo was born and raised in the house in Kratine, which is in the mountains, and he lived there with his family until he was age 10 or thereabouts. And then because of the economy and just difficult circumstances, they moved down into -- to the bottom of the valley. And they just went straight down and they built a house, basically while they were living in it. Now, that's the house of Nadioci and that's where Mr. Bralo lived the remainder of his youth, and he played an increasingly important role in the construction of the house as he grew older. It was an ongoing process. When his family fled Bosnia because of the war, he and his wife stayed behind and they lived in the house in Nadioci. He continued to go to the house in Kratine for many years because his grandmother lived there, but after she died they didn't go up there that often. However, during the war, by helping to hold the Bosnian army at Kratine, he helped protect his father's land and the house in which he was born in Kratine and he was also protecting his family home in Nadioci that he helped to build as a young man. The house was very close, to the defensive lines built just above the family house in Kratine would have had the same -- he would have had the same motivation and -- in terms of wanting to protect his family's holdings. Once again I draw the Chamber's attention to the Celebici Trial Judgement, this time to the Trial Chamber's treatment of one of the Celebici prison guards who had tortured and cruelly treated his own prisoners. And I'm quoting, "The armed conflict created an environment clearly not of Mr. Landzo's own choosing. His home town of Konjic was shell over a continued period of time in 1992 resulting in an atmosphere of constant fear of injury or death for himself or his family, and it was also under a blockade." This kind of personalised treatment of the evidence relating to Mr. Bralo's personal background and prior character is lacking in his Sentencing Judgement. Therefore, we respectfully ask that this honourable Appeals Chamber review these findings and apply the correct relevancy standard as determined under 1.1. And unless there are any questions, I will now give the floor to Mr. Cooper to deal with the question of cooperation at ground 1.2 (B), and the overall assessment of mitigation at ground 1.3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Madam President, Your Honours. I take the floor again to deal with the second part of our second subground of appeal. Your Honours recall that the second subground has this heading, that the Trial Chamber erred by failing to give proper weight to specific factors in mitigating sentence. And the topic at 1.2 (B) is cooperation. Now, Your Honours will be aware that in addition to the pleadings in the opening brief, there are two further supplemental briefs in relation to this. I'm going to start though, if I may, by taking Your Honours to the discussion of cooperation in the Sentencing Judgement. The conclusion which is set out at paragraph 81 is that the Trial Chamber finds that there is not evidence of substantial cooperation from Bralo with the Prosecution. They go on, "There is evidence of some cooperation in the form of provision of documents and a willingness to give information, albeit in a prescribed format." And the Trial Chamber gives that appropriate weight as moderate cooperation. Now, it's worth looking precisely at that because it's possible to be mistaken as to exactly what the finding was. The finding was that, as regards cooperation, there was no substantial cooperation. It was moderate cooperation and, if Your Honours look at paragraph 83, you will see that the Trial Chamber takes into account at subparagraph 5, cooperation with the Prosecution, and in the paragraph that follows goes on to ascribe little weight to that factor. So it's not substantial, it's moderate, and it deserves little weight. That was the finding of the Trial Chamber. Now, it is our submission that the passage that leads up to those conclusions deserves study. It's only an eight-paragraph passage, but our respectful submission is that some of the language in those eight paragraphs is as chaotic as the hearing which dealt with this particular matter at the outset at the sentence hearing. To take a start at the very beginning of paragraph 73, the Judgement starts promisingly. Rule 111 (B) (ii) clearly states, it says and goes on that, "Substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor by convicted person may count as a mitigating circumstance." But of course that's not the test. The test set out and clearly set out in Rule 111 (B) (ii) is that substantial cooperation shall count as a mitigating circumstance. And as one continues to read over the succeeding seven paragraphs, one sees a number of, as we say, errors in the assessment of this evidence. While the Trial Chamber goes on to note our submissions firstly in relation to a number of elements of cooperation, but I have to say it didn't list all of the submissions that were made, or all of the elements that were relied on. The Trial Chamber notes that Mr. Bralo handed over documents to the United Nations authorities in 1997 which had been used in at least one trial. We had at that time been told by the Prosecution of one trial usage and we found out for ourselves a second trial usage. Goes on, "Bralo renders himself compellable before the Tribunal as a witness and has placed no restrictions on the use of the factual basis." Well, that was right, and we had contrasted in the sentencing hearing Mr. Bralo's approach with that of Mr. Simic who, Your Honours will recall, sought a restriction on the use that could be made of his factual basis. And you will recall that he was given credit for his plea notwithstanding that restriction, but was given no additional credit for helping the Prosecution. If that was right, we said at the sentence hearing Mr. Bralo's unrestricted factual basis was deserving of that additional credit which had been denied to Mr. Simic. The Judgement goes on at C, "Bralo has submitted the factual basis with a further detailed statement." That was the document in the sentencing materials at document A2, which was a detailed narrative, statement responding to certain questions that had been asked of him. Goes on at paragraph 74, "He is willing to be questioned by the Prosecution or the Chamber in some formalised way on the record rather than behind closed doors in order to minimise the threat to him and his family's safety that will be consequent at any hint that a private deal had been struck by him with the Prosecution." And that was in effect a proposal for a deposition under Rule 71, as has been used, for example, in the Halilovic case. The Judgement notes, "The Defence finally argued that the factual bases for the plea agreement may be being used in another case, which is not subject to public proceedings," and it sought to know whether this was indeed the case, as it might be evidence that goes to Bralo's cooperation. There will be some more to say about that in a moment. But we pause to note that not every element of cooperation had been identified in that summary. One of the most important was the information given to the Prosecution about Mr. Bralo himself, about his own conduct. It was that information which had informed the wholly new Count 1 about which he had pleaded guilty to in the plea hearing. That had been central to our submissions about cooperation. Also we should say this was an incomplete account because of course there was other material we simply did not know about at that stage. And one of those things was the use that was made, if any use was made, of the factual basis in the Blaskic review proceedings if there were any such review proceedings. Because at the date of the sentencing hearing those matters were not known to the Defendant. The Judgement noted that the Prosecution responded as follows: It argued that the written statement given by Mr. Bralo and appended to the defence brief was incomplete in that there were areas he did not discuss. Well, we note that, but in the context of Mr. Bralo's offering himself for a deposition procedure to answer any questions that anybody had got, the Prosecution, Chamber, or anybody. And the Judgement continued: "The Prosecution further compared the purported cooperation of Bralo with other types of cooperation that it had received from other accused in which original documentation had been provided, the accused person had submitted himself to interviews, and the accused had given actual testimony." In our reply in the sentencing hearing we said in a passage at pages 85 and 86, first the expression I used was a shortfall of logic, there seemed to be something perverse. If the Prosecution really want answers to these questions then why not ask those questions in a formal proceeding? Second, comparing this with other substantial cooperation cases, the three elements that had been mentioned, documents, interview, testimony, well, we had each of those in the present case. Or the very realistic promise of them. The Judgement continues: "There exists therefore a profound difference between the submissions of the Prosecution and the Defence over whether Bralo has provided substantial cooperation that should be taken into account as a mitigating circumstance." It goes on: "This dispute does not concern the facts of what Bralo has done, but, rather, the meaning to be attached to his acts or omissions and the value to be placed on them." Again we all understood that to be the case, that there was no dispute on the fact of the cooperation, but the Trial Chamber and the Defence were wrong because this was not the proper factual basis for assessment of cooperation at all. And it reminded me, when reviewing this material, of an exchange that happened a little earlier in the sentencing hearing when Judge Bonomy said to me, "Now I suspect, Mr. Cooper, at the moment it is as much as you are going to get from this situation and subject to obviously -- to discovering at some later stage that you have been misled, which we have no reason to think is the case." Now, he is referring there to a different matter. He is referring there to the possibility of use in the Blaskic review proceedings. But we certainly did not consider then the likelihood that we had, in fact, been misled as to the available factual material. There was, following a shortfall of logic, a shortfall in disclosure which has now become apparent. And we're grateful for the fact that the Appeals Chamber has put that right with its decision on Rule 115 and its particular observations about the obligation -- particular observations, forgive me, about the obligation to disclose under Rule 68. The Judgement goes on with a proposition which we ourselves had urged that the amount of cooperation given by an accused need not be substantial for it to be taken into account. And it continues: "In the Prosecution's view, cooperation of a nature that should be considered as a factor in mitigation of punishment has not occurred in the present case." We just pause to consider the impact of that statement. Prosecution's view, "cooperation of a nature that should be considered as a factor in mitigation of punishment," has not occurred in the present case. Now we note that that is not the position of the Prosecutor at today's hearing. Mr. Kremer today states that on the material available the accurate designation of the cooperation was moderate. Not nothing, but was moderate. So when asked what's the difference between the factual position before the Trial Chamber as described by the then-Prosecutor, Mr. Harmon, effectively as "nothing," and the position described by Mr. Kremer today as "moderate," given what Your Honours have said about sanctions and the possibility of them under Rule 68, that is a question to which the Appeals Chamber will want an answer. We simply invite you to say that it is impossible to square the facts of the situation at the sentencing hearing which must have been known to the Prosecutor at that time with the representations which were made to the Court on this question. Now, the Judgement continues. "Some documents to the international forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1997 were supplied and they had been used in other proceedings before the Tribunal. The Judgement continued, "Without itself having received this information, it is difficult for the Trial Chamber to assess its quantity and quality but it takes into account its provision nonetheless." Now, we note that that material was predominantly used in closed session in relation to what we understood to be a complex trial which took place not over many months but years. We had sought all the Rule 68 disclosure that we could have and we had been told as recently as the day before the sentence hearing that there was no more material to give. The Defence were simply in no realistic position to advance that proposition further. The Judgement continues: "Finally with regard to the use that may be made of the factual basis, the Trial Chamber finds this is also of limited value as evidence of cooperation. Therefore," he -- it says, "even if the factual basis is being used by the Prosecution, its use does not imbue it with value as evidence of cooperation from Bralo." Now, that appears to indicate not just a burden on the Defendant to shift, to establish this element of mitigation, but a burden which would be a burden with a very high standard in which the Trial Chamber could properly resist a proposition unless it is demonstrated to be a necessary conclusion from the material available. Now, that is far in excess of a standard, of a balance of probabilities. And in our submission the Trial Chamber was perverse to have treated the 1997 documents -- forgive me. I'll pause for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cooper, you have stated a number of things about the cooperation provided by the Appellant to the Prosecution. In the light of the evidence and in the light of the factual findings, how would you qualify the cooperation provided by your client? Is it an extensive, complete cooperation? Are we talking about a moderate cooperation? Or is it weak or extremely weak type of cooperation? I would be grateful if you could give me your assessment of your client's cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. The short answer is we suggest there was substantial cooperation of moderate extent. I'm going to explain both of those if I may in a moment. But we are clear as to the characterisation that we feel was proper and is proper in relation to the cooperation. I was referring to what we regard as a perverse approach by the Trial Chamber, with respect, in treating the 1997 documents in one way, and the 2005 documents in another. The 1997 documents were looked at and their use was considered, but the 2005 documents weren't considered at all. They were simply not relevant to the possible issue of cooperation in the case. And it seemed that the Trial Chamber made itself wilfully blind to the use that might have been made of those documents. Now, one completely understands the position that there was in relation to the secrecy of the Blaskic review proceedings but that, in my submission, is not an excuse for the treatment of this point at that time. I pause just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Schomburg has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam President. [In English] I am afraid you discussed a lot the question of cooperation. You called it substantial, moderate cooperation. I would like you to go a little bit more into details to substantiate this because until now, with all due respect, I regard it only as a gambling with words. What is your assessment of the quantity and the quality of the cooperation? Does it matter whether the same information were used only once or several times? Could you please elaborate on the added value in a concrete case, based on the cooperation of your client, and finally could you please demonstrate a result that emanates from this cooperation of your client? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful for that question, and I will address it immediately, if I may. The first stage has to be: What are the criteria for assessment because the proposal that I make has to be made in light of those particular criteria. And so if I first set out what I respectfully suggest are the appropriate criteria for the assessment cooperation at all and, as I say here, substantial cooperation, I can then address the question that follows, which is: What should be the mitigation effect of substantial cooperation. Is it the same as substantial cooperation or is there a different test that needs to be applied? So the first question is, what are the criteria, what is the definition of cooperation, and of substantial cooperation? Your Honours will have seen briefing in relation to that from both sides. In the most recent briefing from the Prosecution there is a dictionary definition of cooperation which includes working together towards the same end. We checked and found another element of cooperation, which was help provided by doing what is asked or required. And that latter element of the definition may give a clue as to the designation of cooperation that was given by the Prosecutor at the time of the sentencing hearing. Because Mr. Bralo had helped by doing what was asked or required, with the one exception of not having the interview with the Prosecution. He had supplied his additional statement, proffers extensive facts, he had supplied a plea basis that went beyond the crime that was charged, went beyond even the new Count 1, because you will see features in that plea basis which are not required in order to have established even the brand new Count 1. Of course the rest of it that was part of Count 1, much of it was brand new information coming from Mr. Bralo himself. But the plea basis wasn't limited to that which was necessary to prove Count 1. Now, I'm grateful for Your Honour's question, and I'm particularly mindful of Your Honour's words in the Deronjic case of the absolute paramount need in all of this exchange over pleas, plea agreements, consideration, the absolute and paramount consideration is truth. And whatever else happened in -- in particular did not happen in the plea agreement, the watchword was truth, and was always truth in Mr. Bralo's case. To be clear, he had not sought to plead guilty on a restricted basis. He did not seek to bargain away elements of the original indictment. He did not bargain for immunity from prosecution. There had been no bargain at all. His pleas were given voluntarily not as a chip in a bargain but because they were true. And because there were additional matters that were true, they could be included in the factual basis, notwithstanding they weren't strictly necessary for proving Count 1. And when I say "true," I think it is agreed between the parties that there is no instance that the Prosecution point to in the history of this case to indicate Mr. Bralo has ever told a lie. So his situation is perhaps a little different from a number of others who have come before the Court with a plea agreement which causes a Trial Chamber to have a sharp intake of breath to ascertain why it might be that the representatives of the Prosecution would feel it appropriate to reduce charges, change charges, et cetera. Now, that quote that I was referring to from Your Honour, Judge Schomburg, no just -- "no peace without justice; no justice without truth," and that means the entire truth and nothing but the truth, that's a quote that finds reflection in the voices from Ahmici which were included in our sentence brief, individuals who were prepared to speak to the Defendant, to speak to his counsel, to consider his actions and to pass their exceptionally generous judgement about what he had done, expressing gratitude, even admiration, for his stance. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Meron would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Cooper, could we return for a moment to this interview which Mr. Bralo refused to grant the Prosecutor? You argued that there was substantial cooperation. At first blush, it is sort of difficult to reconcile this notion of substantial cooperation with the refusal to meet appropriately with the Prosecutor. One more question after that, but could you start with this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Firstly, in relation to substantial cooperation, the answer is quite simple. There had been a process of exchange of information which had been done through the process of proffers of -- questions being asked by the Prosecution, answers being given, submitted in writing through the lawyers. And that was done. At the time of the plea agreement, what then happened was there was a further factual basis and there was a further statement which, when Your Honours look at it, and I know you will be familiar, starts with a declaration that this was a statement responding to questions asked of me by a number of parties, including the Prosecution. So this was a statement, and we from the papers in elsewhere in relation to other cases that the Prosecution are quite happy to accept statements from defendants in certain circumstances and to use them. Now, the plea agreement was concluded, or the pleas were entered, in mid-July at a time of some sensitivity in relation to the future timing for any review of the Blaskic appeal decision. And during that time there was very heightened excitement in Croatia as to the possibilities that might exist in relation to those who were seen to be assisting the Prosecution. As a result of that, certain press cuttings were supplied by the Prosecutor to us in relation to what was being reported in Croatia as to what Mr. Bralo was said to have been doing with the Prosecution. And I have to say that in relation to both the Prosecution then and myself, we could see that there was some completely speculative, purported information doing the rounds. But there were other matters which appear to have had some basis in documents that should not ever have been disclosed in the public. So amidst the wild speculation that there was, Mr. Bralo's position was, put me, if you will, in the witness box in the courtroom under the cameras, make it closed session if you like, but make it -- make it clear that the fact of my cooperation is a known fact and the record of my testimony will be available to anybody, Prosecution, Defence, appeal, review, Trial Chamber, do it like that. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. Do I remember correctly that over time Mr. Bralo handed over nine documents to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Tell me, counsel, why didn't you put those documents into the trial record of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: The -- we were given some copies which were not legible. We had been put on notice of these materials. They were together with a number of other materials. We made reference to them. We didn't put them actually as an exhibit to our sentence brief. Perhaps we should have done. What we did was made reference. It was agreed between the parties at least to an extent, what had been done with those documents. It was known as one factor of our mitigation. And had there been any question from the Trial Chamber, as there has been a question from this Appeals Chamber, as to, well, what were they, let's have a look at them and what do they show, then they could have been before the Chamber and, in our submission, we were in no position to be able to argue a clear and definitive account as to their significance because of the closed nature of the -- the testimony and the cases that they were used in. I can say that uses are more apparent now partly because we have more access to material, partly because we have had more Rule 68 disclosure. And if it is of assistance, I can supply, in fact, I have handed up already, a little schedule that sets out for each of the documents where we have found there to have been a use by the Prosecution. That should be available before you. And I wonder if that might be the moment now to hand that up and for you to have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cooper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen wishes to ask a question of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Cooper, I have to confess to sharing the average hearer's need for clarification from you of your characterisation of the appellant's cooperation, if I understand you correctly, as substantial but moderate. Now, it may be that you can always bring to bear additional evidence of various kinds to query the Trial Chamber's conclusions. But seeking from you some material amendment of their findings, I would remind you of what the Trial Chamber found and ask you very kindly to indicate what substantial amendment would you make to its findings. Its findings are in paragraph 81 of the Sentencing Judgement. In there it says, "In conclusion the Trial Chamber finds that there is not evidence of substantial cooperation from Bralo with the Prosecution. There is evidence of some cooperation in the form of provision of documents and a willingness to give information, albeit in a prescribed format. And the Trial Chamber gives that appropriate weight as moderate cooperation." The Trial Chamber gives that appropriate weight as moderate cooperation. Now, in what way would you amend the substance of those findings by the arguments you have addressed to the Court this afternoon and in particular with reference to the additional material?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I'm obliged, and forgive me. I've been seeking to address Your Honour, Judge Schomburg's question, and it is now Your Honour's question as well. And I go to it directly. Substantial cooperation of moderate extent, what does that mean? It means this: It appears that the fact that General Blaskic was the commander of the Alpha Force appears to have been provable only through Mr. Bralo's cooperation by the supply of these documents. Now, that was a matter which was relevant to a number of trials, not least his own. Now, why do we know that? We know that because of the new material which has emerged. Because we now know that in relation to the 1997 document from the Prosecution - this was an ex parte document which has been served upon us - this was an assessment by the Prosecution of the significance of these materials in relation to the Blaskic trial. It was, as Your Honours know, a contemporaneous account explaining just why the materials were so important to be admitted. And we can see that in that 1997 document the Prosecution has asked for an ex parte hearing so they can make a complete showing regarding the relevance of the testimony of the officer to whom Mr. Bralo made his initial verbal confession, and also who received those documents. We know that Mr. Blaskic resisted admission of those documents and did so vigorously, and it's not difficult to understand why. Because they showed that he was commander of Alpha Force, that Mr. Bralo was a prominent member thereof, and that served to impeach the claim made by Blaskic that he did not know Bralo. That's the significance which we now understand this document had in relation to the Blaskic trial. When one looks at the schedule that I have provided, hopefully it becomes clearer. Even now I can't say that this is a definitive statement of every use by the Prosecutor or the rationale for every use. That really is a matter specifically in the province of the Prosecution, and we say that once material like this has emerged, once a claim has been made by a Defendant in these circumstances, then the burden must shift to the Prosecution to rebut what is clearly a prima facie case of cooperation. The Defence were in the dark. They were in the dark about most of the -- most of the uses that we now see. In fact, we've remained significantly in the dark, and trying to piece together the uses is a difficult task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cooper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cooper, Judge Guney would like to put a question, one or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cooper, my question now derives from the previous one. And I may be sort of playing or punning on words, but you said that your client's cooperation was substantial, but with a moderate extent. Moderate cooperation cannot be substantial, so I think that there is a contradiction, an obvious contradiction in terms. Would you be kind enough to enlighten us on this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm glad to. And it follows from the submissions that I was making and developing in relation to the appropriate definitions of cooperation and substantial cooperation, and what exactly those terms mean. So I hope Your Honours will bear with me while I address those matters, because the definition that I have urged upon you is not a play on words. These are words of significance, and they are words which will help to determine the appropriate sentence. What I invite Your Honours to do is look at what the test should be for substantial cooperation. Cooperation of substance. And if one has in mind that notion of cooperation of substance, one considers then, is this cooperation which was illusory or worthless, or was it cooperation which led to reliance in a court of law to prove a fact that had to be proved in the most reliable and the most efficient way. If it passes those tests, it must be material of substance. So the starting point has to be: Let's look at the uses, let's look at the schedule, let's see the various uses, and let us say, are these lacking substance or is each of these uses in each of these trials an indicator of substance? So that's the first point. It then follows that -- I'm just going to pause for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cooper, could you finish before the break, but of course you will have an opportunity to be granted a couple of more minutes later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I'm obliged and I hope to be able to do so. Your Honours, I have drawn a distinction between the test for remorse and the test for utility. Remorse is obviously very important, and any cooperation may flow from remorse. But the question of utility is a separate matter, and whilst one might ask questions in relation to remorse, to consider how sorry the Defendant is, how spontaneous, how genuine was his cooperation. When one considers utility, that is a different question. One considers there, was there one document supplied or many documents supplied? Was there use in one trial or many trials? Was this to use -- to prove one thing or many things? Did the document prove a vital fact? Is the cooperation used up or is there a promise of more usable material? Did the material help truth to emerge in the trials? Did it help lies to be challenged? And again, you see from the schedule that in relation to that test of utility it passes all of them. Mr. Bralo scores high on remorse, certainly, but he also scores high in relation to utility. So I concluded with a number of principles on this point of cooperation. Cooperation of substance may be mitigating even when the Defendant lacks remorse, but what must follow is that what cooperation of substance must come in varying degrees. It must come in different sizes, cooperation may be big or may be small. And yet it may still be substantial cooperation, cooperation of substance. Now, no doubt there could have been 200 documents, not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but we have to have a break for technical reasons. How much time do you need to complete your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I think not longer than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will have a break now. The hearing stands adjourned for 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Cooper, we would ask you to complete your submissions within the next 15 minutes, at the most. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Madam President, Your Honours, I'm obliged and I will do so. Your Honours have asked a question about "substantial" and yet also "moderate" at the same time. Let me be clear: I start by addressing the issue of what substantial means. And this is triggered by the Prosecutor saying in his most recent filing that the material supplied by the Defendant was not substantial in any legal sense. And that encouraged us to look again at the law dictionary for a definition of the word "substantial," and we did so. Under the Merriam Webster law dictionary definition for "substantial," the first element is, "of or relating to substance," and you have heard me address that matter, substance, and then, "not illusory, having merit; example: Fail to raise a substantial constitutional claim." That was the first element. The second was, "having importance or significance, being material; example: A substantial step had not been taken towards the commission of the crime." And a separate element was, "Considerable in quantity. Significantly great." And when one looks at the Merriam Webster law dictionary definition, the first element is of quality, the second is of quantity. Now, that's why one can say this was evidence of substantial cooperation. That's because it's a quality test. The first thing is, does it count in law? Did it do something in the trials? Did it supply something that was necessary? Was it of substance? Yes or no. The next question is the volume of it, and no amount of volume will help if the material lacks the essential quality of substance. And so when I say "substantial cooperation," I address firstly quality. These were central documents which were used again and again and again, not just in one trial but in many. They were significant. They were relied on by the Prosecution for specific purposes. They fought against resistance from Defendants to have these materials admitted. They argued contemporaneously for the value of those documents. They argued in 1997, in the Cayley memorandum; they argued in 2005, in the Blaskic review application; and they argued again in the reply. They argued, the Prosecution argued the significance of this material. There can be no question that this material passes the test of substance, the test of quality. When it comes to quantity, well, that is a different matter. There would have been more quantity if there had been 200 documents. There would have been more quantity if they had been used in 50 trials, not four. That's why we say the first -- the first element has to be quality, and yes it passes that test. And it well passes that test and it did at the time of the sentencing hearing. And secondly, there is the question of quantity, and we say that this was significant. We say that it was moderate in volume of substantial cooperation. And actually, there is a third element to think about as well. And that is the element of how much mitigation should be credited for this given material. Now, that doesn't strictly follow from the definition of any material as substantial cooperation, as the international authorities and the domestic authorities show. In particular, Your Honours will have seen that the rationale for giving mitigation is frequently to reflect the danger that a Defendant puts himself in, in supplying material that can help the Prosecution authorities. And the greater the danger, the greater the risk, the greater the credit that is often given for domestic authorities for that cooperation. Not simply utility in other proceedings but also coming back and looking at the Defendant himself. So if documents were giving spontaneously in a volatile situation, if the fact of his giving the documents became notorious, if there were immediate fears for the safety of the donor, well, all of those would be matters relevant to the amount of credit that should be given to him for supplying the documents in those circumstances. And when one looks at the Bralo situation, they were given in a spontaneous situation in 1997 by a volunteer who simply approached UN forces with a bundle of documents, making an oral statement, and also supplying the documents. And as we set out in the sentencing brief, you will have seen the memo by Human Rights Watch to Madeline Albright asking her to raise her concerns to the Croatian government about the safety and the whereabouts of Miroslav Bralo when he had been taken into custody following the volatile situation in Vitez in 1997, in which it became known, as it did very swiftly, that - there is a reference to a Washington Post article in 1997 - that these documents had been supplied and by Miroslav Bralo. So all of those matters are, in our submission, relevant. Firstly, was there substance; secondly, assess the volume; and third, assess the credit that should properly be given to the person who supplied them in the circumstances that they did. Your Honours, that completes what I have to say about the second subhead of appeal, and I can deal briefly with the third subhead. That's the overall reduction for mitigation. Your Honours, we invite your ruling that the Trial Chamber erred by failing to order an appropriate reduction of sentence, to reflect the mitigation of the case at it was at the sentence hearing, in light of the detailed factors that we set out and the grounds with which you're familiar. In any event, there will need to be a reassessment of the sentence in the light of the new material in the case, although, as we say, there won't be a need for a complete rehearing unless the Appeals Chamber is to embark on that course yourselves. Now, we accept that there was powerful material on both sides. We don't contest the starting point for this sentence, including aggravating features of as high as 25 years. Equally, however, we submit that the mitigation, when properly evaluated according to correct legal principle, and in light particularly of the policy imperatives that we set out in our appeal brief drawing, and we're grateful from the utterances of Your Honour, Judge Meron and Your Honour Judge Schomburg, we say that this mitigation was worth a greater reduction from that starting point. And the principal reason was the finding of genuine remorse. Conceded by the Prosecution -- not conceded, accepted, recognised by the Prosecution, and endorsed by the Trial Chamber. It is from that source of genuine remorse that everything else that's good about this case has flowed. Now, we made our submissions about totality of sentence in our sentencing brief as to the reduction that we urged was appropriate. And what did we have in mind? We had in mind a number of cases in the ICTY case law. The case of Ademovic, a man like the Defendant, motivated to confess spontaneously when not under arrest, a man who said that he could not live with his conscience, the words could have been identical. They are virtually identical to those used by Mr. Bralo in 1997 standing in a UN compound in Vitez. His sentence: 10 years. We are aware also of the sentence of Mr. Deronjic, a sentence of 10 years, despite, and one notes, being a high-ranking perpetrator committing heinous and long-planned crimes. We're aware of the Plavsic sentence of 11 years, but nevertheless, we ourselves proposed the starting point as comparison should be the Kordic and the Santic trial sentences at 25 years, setting a starting point including aggravating circumstances. We noted Santic's sentence reduction following his partial cooperation and his limited remorse, following as it did upon a fully contested trial, and we noted the consequent reduction to 18 years, despite the Appeals Chamber having considerable scepticism, as they said, about certain aspects of the case. We respectfully propose to the Trial Chamber a shorter sentence than Santic's resultant sentence of 18 years. And in respect to that case, if the only difference between the 25-year trial sentence and the 18-year sentence, is Santic's very belated remorse, it shows that the reduction in this case, in the light of all the exceptional circumstances, was out of step. Mr. Bralo had pleaded guilty, unlike his commander Santic. He had done so way, way before trial. Well before ever arriving at this Tribunal, he had pleaded guilty with his admission against his interest to UN forces in 1997. That was genuine, expressed spontaneously and effectively all that time ago. His efforts to engage now with the present-day practical realities in Ahmici through his counsel, and the touching statements that had been contributed on his behalf from the Bosniak community there were a wholly remarkable testament of hope which, we submitted, deserved to be reflected in a substantial reduction of sentence to enable and to encourage those initiatives to proceed. Your Honours, this element of our appeal was extensively covered in our written briefing. We will assist you on this of course or on any points if Your Honours have questions. But that's how we put our submissions on appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cooper. Judge Shahabuddeen would like to put one or two questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One question by way of comparing notes. I understand you and it makes sense to me now that I have listened to you and reflected on what you have said that the cooperation of your client was substantial in degree but moderate in extent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I am obliged. If only I had that formula, it would have saved some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now give the floor to the Prosecution for the presentation of the response of the Prosecution. Mr. Kremer, are you going to speak on behalf of the Prosecution? You have the floor in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. I had proposed in our preliminary discussions with our team to start and review and present an overview of the principles of sentencing, including a standard of review, and focus on the gravity of the crimes. But given the time spent by my colleagues opposite on other matters, I thought that we would change the order.
