I'm going to ask Ms. Carey to speak first on cooperation and use, which appears to be of a matter of significant interest to this panel, and then Mr. Tracol will deal with the personal circumstances and issues falling under ground one, and I will then sum up and address the questions of the gravity of the circumstances, the remorse, and the treatment of mitigating circumstances in a -- in the global context. So that is the way we propose to proceed, and I will turn the podium over to Ms. Carey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have the floor, Ms. Carey.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Before beginning my principal submissions, I would like to make just a few preliminary points. Following from my learned colleague's submissions, I think that there was a theme in this case, and that theme is transfiguration. You might note from the submissions that the original submissions of my learned colleague were that there was cooperation with the Tribunal; those were his submissions at sentence, those were his submissions in the appeal brief. Now the submissions have transfigured themselves to become substantial cooperation with the Prosecution. Now, I note that this is a theme because you will also have heard that during the course of his submissions, he mentioned that the factual basis was actually a statement, a statement made by the accused, to the Prosecution and that that came through the proper process. Now, I'd like to just point out what the proper process was like. The proper process is one that takes place without prejudice. It did not lead to a plea that identified the scope and degree of cooperation that the accused would provide with the Prosecution. It led only to the guilty plea that you have in front of you. Now, this plea of guilty is one that pleas to the basic facts, those are which required for the Trial Chamber to have found him guilty of the crimes charged. The factual basis includes facts from the indictment principally and then some additional facts. And I would ask Your Honours to look at the factual basis in conjunction with the indictment, and I think that you will find that those additional facts, far from being as characterised by my learned friend, actually principally limit the involvement of Mr. Bralo in the crimes charged. They limit his involvement to that of an aider and abettor in one case. They -- the additional facts state that he acted under orders and that he was a victim as a weapon of war. That supported his submission, that he was a victim as a weapon of war. This process cannot be equated with a statement which is a full and frank accounting of the information that a Defendant has before to the authorities. In fact this was an exchange between the attorneys to get to the point where a guilty plea could be entered. There is a great distinction between that and that which has been undertaken by other accused before this Tribunal who have gotten credit for making statements to the Prosecution. I would also like to point out preliminarily that he also mentioned that one other way to define cooperation was help provided by doing what was asked or required. But that's precisely the Prosecution's point in this case. The reason that it initially made its submission that there was not substantial cooperation, and why it still believes that there was not, was because Mr. Bralo did not do what he was asked to do and, given the extent of the assistance that he could have given, did not do what was required. I would also like to point out that it was mentioned that one must distinguish the test for remorse for the test for utility as follows. This was one statement made: "The utility need not be spontaneous or genuine like remorse." But, in fact, we submit that it does. Now I will move to my principal submissions. The information from Bralo and its use by the Prosecution merited credit only as moderate cooperation. The use of this information by the Prosecution is evidence of the quality of the cooperation of the accused. It is not evidence of cooperation itself. To determine the extent of cooperation, a Chamber has to assess the cooperation's quantity and quality. Now, quantity is obvious; that equals size. But I think that you also have to look within that at two points, an objective point and a subjective point: How much was offered and how much could have been given. Now, quality, that requires the weighing of a number of factors. The accuracy of the information, the timeliness in which the information was given, and the utility of the information to the Prosecution. In considering utility, there are several additional considerations. Does the information concern only the conduct of the accused himself, or does it contain -- concern other potential targets or avenues of investigation? Does this information provide greater context for events of interest to other investigations and other cases? Does it represent information that's not currently in the possession of the Prosecution or does it help confirm existing evidence or corroborate existing witnesses? The fact that a piece of information has been used is evidence of the utility of that information. Agreed. This in turn may demonstrate that this aspect of cooperation is of sufficient quality. But then this aspect of cooperation has to be considered in conjunction with any other forms of cooperation that has been provided by the accused, such as testimony or statements. A Chamber then has to consider the overall accuracy, timeliness, and utility, as well as completeness of the cooperation bundle. Now, for that cooperation bundle to be substantial, it principally must be a full and frank accounting of what the accused knows. This evaluative method is evidenced in domestic legal systems that have considered substantial assistance with authorities as mitigation of sentence. I draw your attention the case of of R versus A and B. This is a case coming from the United Kingdom that is cited in our book of authorities, and I will quote from that case. "Value is a function of quality and quantity. If the information is accurate, particularised, useful in practice and hitherto unknown to the authorities, enabling serious criminal activity to be stopped and serious criminals to be brought to book, the discount may be substantial."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Merci, Madam President. Counsel, turning to specifics which you have now just mentioned, the counsel for Mr. Bralo referred to -- argued that it was on the basis of information provided by his client that it was established that General Blaskic was commander of Alpha Force. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: The information provided by Mr. Bralo did confirm that Blaskic was the commander of Alpha Force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: How important was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: That was one element of a massive case against Mr. Blaskic. It principally, and I believe that my learned friend did mention this, the primary use of the evidence provided by Mr. Bralo was, in fact, to impeach Mr. Blaskic's own testimony, which was that he did not know Bralo. Now, I will allow to weigh for yourself, because I know you were all aware with the Blaskic case, whether or not that was -- that was the most significant fact. The Prosecution is not submitting that the provision of the documents was not useful to the Prosecution. That is not our claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But it appears from what you have now explained that it was also useful in the very specific sense of relating to the role of a very important person, General Blaskic, in the events, and, incidentally, one which I would be extremely grateful, since I have the pleasure of talking to you now, which is not clear quite to me. I don't understand why communications at trial about Prosecution's reliance on Bralo's materials were presented as ex parte communications. It would have seemed to me that those communications should have been inter partes, but confidential, to allow Bralo a right of response while preserving the necessary confidentiality. Can you enlighten me, why was this ex parte?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: If you will allow me just one second. It is my understanding and that has been confirmed that there was an order present that maintained the complete confidentiality, secrecy, of those proceedings. I believe that I am not in the position to second guess the Trial Chamber or my -- or the Prosecution in that moment, but I do believe that the reason that an ex parte filing was made was to try to apprise the Trial Chamber of the situation, and that at least obliquely that fact was communicated to the Defence so that all would understand that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: If I may return to my submissions now. Turning also to a case cited from Canada, with respect to what was -- what is required to demonstrate quantity and quality sufficient for -- to find -- to make a finding of substantial assistance with the Prosecution. In that case the court held that what was -- is to be encouraged is a full and frank cooperation on the part of the offender, whatever be his motive. The extent of the discount will depend to a large extent upon the willingness with which the disclosure is made. The court also found no discount appropriate when an accused tailors his disclosure to reveal only the information which he knows is already in the possession of the authorities, and finally held that the discount will rarely be substantial unless the offender discloses everything that he knows. These cases and those authorities relied upon by the Prosecution and placed in our book of authorities are in harmony with this Tribunal's prior Judgements finding substantial cooperation. In the Tribunal cases where substantial cooperation has been found, all of the accused gave at least one interview to the Prosecution. Miroslav Deronjic, for example, gave 17 interviews for the Prosecution; six when he was a witness and 11 after he was sitting in the Detention Centre. All of the accused made an express agreement to cooperate further with the Prosecution. Most agreed to testify and have testified in at least one trial. Several have provided important documentation. But I would point out that no prior case has found substantial cooperation, absent an interview and an agreement to cooperate. And no prior case has found substantial cooperation on the basis of provision of documents alone. Now, what were the steps taken to cooperate in this case? Unlike the Tribunal cases identified in Annex A to the second supplemental response brief, there was no agreement from Bralo to cooperate. What Bralo has done in this case is provided nine documents, provided a factual basis as part of his guilty plea, to which he attached no limitations as to its further use, and agreed to testify truthfully to the contents of the factual basis, if compelled, and to provide a deposition if ordered. The Prosecution acknowledges and has accepted each of these acts of cooperation as true, but what Bralo has not done has been to participate in a full and frank interview with the Prosecution. Bralo has not provided accurate, particularised information which is useful in practice which was hitherto unknown to the Prosecution. In fact, he has provided little more than the minimum information required for the Trial Chamber to accept his guilty plea. Bralo has not agreed to testify voluntarily, nor has he testified at any trial. And Mr. Bralo has not provided timely information. All of the related cases before this Tribunal, the Furundzija case, the Blaskic case, the Kordic and Cerkez case, the Kupreskic case, were either finished or in the process of being sent back to Bosnia and Herzegovina, pursuant to 11 bis - that would be the Ljubicic case - at the time the factual basis was made. Six of the nine documents received from Bralo in 1997 by UNPROFOR were received independently by the Prosecution from another source in 2003. Thus the only use of Bralo's information after the time that he turned himself in to the Tribunal, was in the Blaskic review proceeding. And that use was of very limited scope. And I'd like to take you through that use. It was used to corroborate other witnesses. It was used to resolve minor inconsistencies between Bralo's information and the information of others. It was used by the Prosecution to reach a single conclusion in the Blaskic review proceeding, and that was, quoting paragraph 177 of the public filing, "At some stage Miroslav Bralo, who had been released from prison joined the group in the Bungalow. Each one of these uses are drawn from two paragraphs in the factual basis, and those paragraphs are paragraph 7 and paragraph 9. The inclusion of the same documents used in Blaskic on the 65 ter list in Ljubicic is not, in the Prosecution submission, a use. Being listed on a 65 ter exhibit list demonstrates no more than an intention of possible future use by the Prosecution. Therefore, this material, this information, does not materially advance or affect any assessment of the Prosecution's reliance on the documents. This same reasoning applies to the fact that the same four documents used in Blaskic and the Bralo plea package were included in a bundle of materials that was transferred to the state prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina pursuant to 11 bis. This again doesn't demonstrate use by the Prosecution; it's a reference to information. Therefore, taken as a whole, the acts of assistance by Bralo were limited in nature. They did not constitute a full and frank accounting of all that he knew and they were not made in a timely manner with respect to related cases. Thus, even when you consider them in light of the use that has been made of them by the Prosecution, these acts can only be seen to have the quality and quantity required for a characterisation of moderate cooperation. This characterisation is consonant with prior Tribunal cases and with the principles that are set out in domestic jurisdictions that employ the guilty plea. And I now stand available for your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Schomburg has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam President. [In English] My question refers to a short remark you made recently. Am I correct in believing that based on the compelling evidence adduced in particular the Blaskic and Kordic trial case, there was more or less no way out for Mr. Bralo but either to flee or to stand trial and surrender, as he did. But the evidence as such was already available from the other cases in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would be correct. That is also -- that would -- that determination would also have been assisted by the Furundzija case, which identified specific criminal conduct of Mr. Bralo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen has a question to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Carey, I was interested in your description of the case against you as a case based on transfiguration. I thought you had in mind that your colleague, across the will of the Court, was saying initially that there was cooperation with the Tribunal and that latterly he altered his language so as to plead cooperation with the Prosecutor. Now, the Tribunal, as we know, is a Hydra-headed creature, so the question in my mind is when the Defence spoke of cooperation with the Tribunal, should we give credit to the Defence for meaning by that the appropriate organ of the Tribunal which in this case and from all that you have said means really the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: In answer to Your Honour's question, I think a review of the participation at the hearing and of the sentencing brief would indicate that that was not -- that this more of a tactical decision. It was known at the time of the sentencing before the sentencing brief and hearing that the Prosecution was not going to make a representation, that there had been substantial cooperation. It would take me a moment to find the references in the hearing, but at the time of the hearing, when Mr. Harmon for the Prosecution began to make his submissions with respect to substantial cooperation with the -- with the Prosecution, the Defence stood and reminded the Court that actually they were not seeking that ruling at this time, that they were seeking a ruling of cooperation with the Tribunal which struck broader. So I think we have to take them on their words on that, because it did appear that the Trial Chamber might have been confused and that they took the opportunity to clarify that point to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask a second question --

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- which is like this: I understood you to be speaking about the handing over by the Prosecution to Bosnia-Herzegovina of certain documents presented to you by the Appellant. And the impression I have is that it was your thesis that that handing over of documents was not really part of any cooperation by the Appellant with the Prosecutor. Would that be correct? Would you not be handing over the documents to Bosnia-Herzegovina in aid of a Prosecution that you would otherwise have to undertake?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, taking that question, the last portion first, it is true that pursuant to 11 bis we turn cases over to the national governments that would otherwise fall within our jurisdiction. And it is certainly true that when we turn over materials to them in support of cases we turn over everything that we believe could have -- could have the potential to aid them. In this case, what was turned over was, in addition to a great deal of other material, everything relating to the related cases so that the -- the cases related to Ljubicic so they could have the context and all the materials that had been adduced. It would not be the Prosecution's position that the materials provided by Miroslav Bralo could have no utility whatsoever, but that this is something that has been -- is being counted again and again and again, and that it doesn't rise to the level, I think, believing -- calling upon my learned friend's definition of things that -- that really get to the truth of the matter and have real substance, counting the same use over and over would seem not to merit that -- that that allocation of substantive. The act of turning it over, the fact that it could be useful, yes, that deserves weight. But counting it in multiple cases seems not to deserve that similar weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Carey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Meron has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, could you perhaps enlighten me a tiny bit on this. Apart from use of information or documents provided by Bralo, which you used in 11 -- the Prosecution used in 11 bis cases, there was some use of that information also in cases before the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Also, we would appreciate it that the Tribunal as a whole has commitments to provide evidence and information to cases which we transferred under our Rules and Security Council Resolutions to Sarajevo under 11 bis. So having information which is based on information provided by Mr. Bralo is in a way -- in some way at least helpful to the Prosecution: It saves them work. But one thing that is again not very clear to me is your reply to my learned colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen, on transfiguration. Now, what I would be interested in knowing, how would you -- if you were a Defendant, how would you cooperate with the Tribunal without actually going through the Prosecutor? Isn't it in most criminal jurisdictions the fact that a Defendant which provides information which deals with guilty pleas, whatever, his contact is the Prosecutor? So what's -- what's so special about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I'm not entirely clear about the second part of that question. The position of the Prosecution with respect to the representations made about the -- about cooperation with the Tribunal was that, actually, you need to look to the submissions of the Defence in this case with respect to that, because they did actually make submissions with respect to cooperation that went beyond acts involving the Prosecution, and that that was precisely their point. They called this cooperative value to the Prosecution, the international Tribunal, and the people of Ahmici, and they did under -- they did, of course, incorporate within that the items of cooperation which they are now representing are of sufficient quality and quantity to be substantial cooperation with the Prosecution, but they incorporated other aspects which did not relate to any relationship between Mr. Bralo and the Prosecution but, in fact, related to saving the Tribunal itself the cost and expense of trial and the -- the - I'm just having to flip through, I'm afraid - his non-adversarial stance in the initial proceedings, and his assistance to the people of Ahmici. Those were his submissions, and they were -- it was not my point to be making to say that there was no place for his contributions to the Prosecution within that larger submission, but that, in fact, it was their submissions that it had been larger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: If there are no further questions, I will allow my colleague, Mr. Tracol, to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tracol, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, Your Honours, I'm now going to respond to the submissions of the Defence, and in particular to the submissions made by Ms. Lindsay. First of all, with regard to the first subground of appeal, related to the fact that mitigating circumstances were not taken into account properly, the position of the Prosecution is that the Trial Chamber properly assessed the arguments of the Defence, including the degrading and deteriorating political and military circumstances in Vitez, the attack against the home of Miroslav Bralo and his wife, the fact that he was released from prison on condition that he join the special unit of the Dzokeri, and the fact that Miroslav Bralo was acting duress under the orders of superior orders [as interpreted]. According to us, the Trial Chamber properly used, exercised its discretion when it accorded only a limited weight or no weight to each one of these factors. Miroslav Bralo has demonstrated no error committed by the Trial Chamber in the exercise of its discretion. Ms. Lindsay stated that the Trial Chamber illegally took into account double -- twice the aggravating circumstances, and I would like to deal with the methodology to be used in that respect. First of all, the Trial Chamber has to examine the gravity of the crime. By far this is the most significant factor when determining -- when setting a fair and just sentence. The notion of gravity encompasses two concepts. First of all, the seriousness of the crime and the mode of commission of the crime. The Trial Chamber must then examine aggravating circumstances, and these can be used in either of two ways. First of all, once an assessment of the gravity of a criminal conduct has been made, any aggravating factor can serve to increase the sentence. Alternatively, where the criminal conduct is so grave that it already merits the highest sentence, aggravating circumstances are not applied to increase the sentence, but can be used to negate the potential effect on sentence of any mitigating circumstances, and that's precisely what the Trial Chamber has done in this particular case. Let me now respond to the various factors raised by Ms. Lindsay, starting with the deteriorating political and military situation in Vitez. According to the Prosecution the Trial Chamber was right in concluding that the deteriorating situation was not a mitigating circumstance in this case. Contrary to what the Defence states, this factor was properly examined. It acknowledges so itself in its brief on appeal. The Trial Chamber has held that this was not a mitigating circumstance after having carefully reviewed the record and contrary to what the Defence states the -- the Trial Chamber has indeed conducted an examination. In that respect the Trial Chamber also quite rightly concluded that no weight should be given to the circumstance. No discernible error was committed by the Trial Chamber in the use of its discretion. And in that respect, if we compare what was held in other cases, Celebici, Aleksovski, Blaskic, we find no support to the arguments put by the Defence according to which an unfair decision was made, because these are cases that encompass different circumstances and different facts that were assessed in a different manner by other Trial Chambers. Because of the gravity of the crimes committed by Miroslav Bralo in this case, the Trial Chamber was right in concluding that the context in which these crimes were committed should not be seen as a mitigating circumstance. In conflict, all the soldiers are faced with difficult decisions. This should not be seen as an excuse, as a pretext to commit crimes such as the brutal crimes that were committed in this case. Although the situation, the political and military situation in Vitez was deteriorating, and we acknowledge that, the general circumstances should not mitigate the sentence passed against Bralo for having killed five persons, as well as for having brutally and repeatedly raped Witness A on the 15th of May, 1993. By their very nature of -- the violations of international humanitarian law only occurred during international -- during armed conflict. The broader context of ethnic tension and war, which sometimes include the commission of crimes on both sides, should not constitute a mitigating circumstance. According to us, the contrary conclusion would imply the application of this mitigating circumstance to any person who commits a war crime or a crime against humanity, with the subsequent absurd result that violations of international humanitarian law would in themselves justify a lower sentence. This is not the message you want to send. The general consideration of the conflict does not constitute a mitigating circumstance. Now, with regard to the second factor of the attack on the home of Bralo and on his wife, here again, according to us, the Trial Chamber was right in finding that this was not a mitigating circumstance in this particular case. Here again the Trial Chamber has properly assessed the personal circumstances of Miroslav Bralo and this particular attack. And the Trial Chamber properly applied its discretion when finding that no weight should be given to this factor. The Trial Chamber therefore made no discernible error in this case when holding that this was not a mitigating circumstance. Let me conclude by stating that Ms. Lindsay said that Miroslav Bralo's superiors had knowledge of this attack and of the reaction of Bralo to this attack, but if you look at the record you find no evidence -- according to us, no evidence that the superiors of Bralo had knowledge of the attack and of the reaction of Miroslav Bralo to this attack. Now, with regard to the conditions in which Bralo was released from prison, here again the Trial Chamber quite rightly held that the pressure that was put to bear on Miroslav Bralo so that he became a member of the Dzokeri, and it took -- to take an active part in the fighting should not be seen as a mitigating circumstance. The Defence has demonstrated no discernible error committed by the Trial Chamber in the exercise of its discretion. Here again let's come back to the facts adduced at trial. There is no single trace of a threat. Quite to the contrary. In paragraph 7 of the statement by Miroslav Bralo, we can read the following, and I quote this in English. "[In English] He told me that it had been sent by Vladimir Santic and that I would be leaving the prison that night if I agreed to fight." If I agreed to fight. [Interpretation] Madam President, Your Honours, the recruit -- the enlistment of Miroslav Bralo, according to his own statement, to the words that he uses, was a condition to his agreement. If he had failed to agree, he would not have been listed among the Jokers. Therefore, the Prosecution cannot agree with a Defence when it is stated as by

utterances.speaker: MS. LINDSAY
utterances.text: He was not a free agent. With regard to the allegations that people of authority would have given specific tasks to Miroslav Bralo. Here, again, in our view, the Trial Chamber quite properly exercised its discretion in deciding to grant no weight at all to the Defence argument, as you heard earlier on today, that Miroslav Bralo was manipulated into committing crimes under superior orders. The Defence merely repeated arguments made at trial. In our view, the Defence failed to identify any discernible error allegedly committed by the Trial Chamber in exercising its discretion. The Defence failed to demonstrate on the balance of probabilities, which is the factor of the test applicable to mitigating circumstances, is no proof at all that he was manipulated by his superiors. There is nothing to indicate, contrary to what the Defence stated, that his superiors knew of his prior conduct; this is the reason why he was recruited. Let me now briefly turn to the second subground of the Defence appeal as to the weight given by the Trial Chamber to various mitigating circumstances. In our view, the Trial Chamber properly assessed the various circumstances; regarding his circumstances, his personal circumstances, committed no discernible error in granting the weight it gave to those mitigating circumstances. This is why we also submit that this appeal should be -- this ground should be dismissed. As to his personal circumstance, family circumstances, the Defence identified various circumstances in this respect. And the Trial Chamber allegedly failed to grant any weight or very -- enough weight to such circumstances. But if you read the Trial Judgement closely, you will see that the Trial Chamber looked into each and every of the circumstances, granting it proper weight. Once again, the Defence failed to prove that the Trial Chamber would have made any discernible error. In our view, it did not abuse its discretion. All of the evidence adduced by the Defence at trial was -- was duly examined by the Trial Chamber, including Miroslav Bralo's childhood. The Defence referred to it earlier on, and also the circumstances in which he was enlisted into the HVO. The Defence is also asking you to reduce this sentence because he lost his job, in view of the difficult situation after the break-up of the former Yugoslavia. In reply, more specifically paragraph 21.2, the Defence mentioned Annex B 4, footnote 21, which is a statement by Farid Ahmic; however, if you look into it, there is nothing to substantiate the Defence allegation as to Miroslav Bralo's loss of work. But it is interesting to look again into his statement, more specifically in paragraph 1, which says the following, and I quote in English again. "[In English] I left my work to join the Vitez reserve police force, and then a short time later a special HVO unit called the Alpha Force." [Interpretation] Things are clear. He voluntarily left his work in order to join the armed forces. In his reply brief in paragraph 21.3, the Defence claimed that the family home of Bralo was on a moving front-line between 1991 and 1994. Once again, the evidence the Defence referred to do not substantiate such a claim. Reference is made to transcripts; however, if you look at them, this is Mark Harmon pleading -- Mark Harmon's pleading -- closing arguments, and they do not substantiate this at all. And there is an annex C, but there are eight C annexes in the trial record, and nothing substantiates the Defence's claim. So you have two examples of claims made by the Defence in their reply brief that have failed to be proved. Madam President, Your Honours, I will now conclude and, of course, I am available for any questions you may have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Tracol, I understood you to be giving no credit to the proposition from the other side that the Appellant was used as a tool by his superiors. If that impression of mine is correct, would it be pertinent to qualify that impression a little by what is stated in paragraph 56, three lines from the bottom. There the Trial Chamber said: "It may be the case that Bralo was used by his superiors as a weapon of war." Now, may it then be better to say that the Trial Chamber recognised that Bralo was used as a tool but that it took account of that when it said, "Once again the Trial Chamber finds that this has no bearing upon the appropriate punishment that he should receive for his crimes." Then in paragraph 54 above, the last sentence reads, "All of his actions display his complete contempt at the time for the laws governing armed conflict, along with a shocking disregard for the value of human life and dignity." In other words, is it right to say that Bralo was never used as a tool by his superiors? Would it be better to say that, yes, he was used as a tool but that the Trial Chamber took account of that and disregarded it for the reasons stated in the various paragraphs which I have read?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 56 of the Trial Judgement, the Trial Chamber expressed the possibility that Bralo was possibly used as a tool, as a weapon of war by his superiors. In so doing, the Trial Chamber therefore identified this factor as a potential mitigating circumstance. However - and that's the second step in the reasoning - when it came to assessing this mitigating circumstance, the Trial Chamber held that this factor could only be granted a limited weight in the light of the seriousness of the crimes that why committed, in light of the circumstances in which the crimes were committed. The heinous type, the very grave type of those crimes committed. In the Prosecution's point of view, the Trial Chamber duly took the mitigating factor into account, but, when comparing it the gravity of the crime and with the aggravating circumstances, decided to grant it only limited weight. This is the way I read the Trial Judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Tracol. I think there's no further questions to be asked of you. Mr. Kremer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I will try to be brief and concise. In summation, our position is that Bralo's sentence of 20 years is low by any standard, particularly when one applies the standard of this Tribunal that the gravity of the crimes and the role of the accused are the primary factors in sentencing. This is no ordinary case. The name Miroslav Bralo was well known to the Tribunal, as Judge Schomburg correctly pointed out, in several case that is had been decided previously. And the degree of brutality that he inflicted on his victims was also well known. And the impact on the victims was staggering and the Trial Chamber reviewed, from paragraphs 24 to 41, the gravity of the crimes and the aggravating circumstances. And if you look at paragraph 28 and following on the nature of the crimes, it is not moderate words that are used. Extreme words are used to describe his crimes. "Crimes of which Bralo was -- has been convicted are of utmost gravity," paragraph 28. Paragraph 29: "Beyond the inherently shocking nature of these crimes, the Trial Chamber takes account of the specific manner in which they were committed by Bralo." On the morning of the day he got there, he participates in the killing of a young Muslim woman with a knife. Her parents had been killed by his colleagues with revolvers. He also shot and killed an unidentified male. He set fire to many houses in Ahmici. He aided and abetted others to set fire to houses in Ahmici, and he participated personally in the destruction of the mosque. And he aided and abetted another member of the HVO in killing 14 members of two Bosnian Muslim families. I'm going to get to this in a moment, but these facts, with the exception of Bralo's involvement in setting of the fires in Ahmici, was all known to the Tribunal and to the Prosecution well in advance of Bralo's guilty plea. As Judge Schomburg correctly points out, Bralo had a stark choice to make when he surrendered himself to the Tribunal. He could plead guilty to the crimes or he could go on trial. Or he perhaps could face transfer to Sarajevo for trial in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The evidence of the scope of the information held by the Prosecution is in the briefs that were filed at sentencing. Attachment B to the Prosecution's sentencing brief, pages 4 to 6, a 1994 UN commission of expert -- reports on the staggering devastation in Ahmici where over a hundred people are killed, 180 homes are destroyed, the mosque is destroyed and hundreds of people are driven from their homes. The Blaskic Trial Judgement speaks paragraphs about what happened in Ahmici under the Jokers and other people who participated in its attack. There is even a specific reference to Ciko [sic], who is Bralo's nickname at paragraph 472. There is the Kordic Trial Judgement, pages 602 to 642, where Bralo is specifically mentioned at pages -- of paragraphs 625 and 626. And in 1997, the Washington Post article that is referred to by Mr. Cooper, attachment C7, which he filed as part of his material, as page 4 contains the following statement: "Last spring the Tribunal spent much effort convincing NATO to remove landmines from an area in Central Bosnia where Bralo was believed to have buried some of his victims, two families and -- with small children. The small children were -- and the two families, were the ones set out in the persecution count, Count 1. And I remind Your Honours that nine young children were --- under the age of 18, were killed by -- by the group that Bralo was with on that day and to which he pleaded guilty. And if you look in the UN commission of experts report in the pages that I have described, you will see that the number of children killed in Ahmici is, I think, 14, if my memory serves me correctly, so that most of the children killed were killed by this group with which Mr. Bralo found himself at the beginning of the attack. Now, in the appeal brief, and I think it's critical that we address this because it shows what Mr. Bralo was attempting to do, and which touches on whether his remorse and whether his cooperation is, in fact, sincere. There are two statements at 36.1 and 36.2 of the appeal brief. First, 36.1, the killing of Mirnesa Salkik [phoen] committed under orders from and in the presence of four more senior soldiers. There is no evidence in the trial record that there were orders given by them to him and that there were four more senior soldiers. And I refer you simply to paragraph 52 of the -- of the sentencing brief -- of the -- of Bralo, where -- and paragraph 8 of the factual basis, where Bralo admits, Bralo "killed Mirnesa Salkik using a knife because he did not have an MGV gun." That's what he admitted to. He didn't admit to being under orders, and he didn't admit to being -- receiving those orders from four senior members or senior soldiers. But more striking is 36.2. The rape of victim -- of Witness A committed on the express instruction of and in the presence of the senior officer Antonio Furundzija. This statement is simply not accurate. I refer you back to paragraph 60 of Bralo's sentencing brief and paragraph 27 of the factual basis. I won't read them, because I think it's more helpful for me to read for you with limited time, paragraph 130 of the Furundzija Trial Judgement, which is the adjudicated fact as to what actually happened. Quote, "There is no doubt that the Accused and the Accused B," which is Bralo, "as commanders divided the process of interrogation by performing different functions. The role of the Accused was to question while accused Bralo" -- or Accused B, which is Bralo's role, "was to assault and threaten in order to elicit the required information from Witness A and Witness D." Your Honours may also wish to read carefully the details of the evidence summarised in the Furundzija Judgement in at paragraphs 70 to 89, the factual findings in 124 to 130, and the legal findings from 262 to 267, to show exactly the case that the Prosecution had against Mr. Bralo, why it wasn't cooperation that was making him plead guilty; it was that he had no other choice. And the shifting position of Mr. Bralo from his original guilty plea to the appeal is exemplified by the mischaracterisation of paragraph 1 of the -- or Count number 1 of the indictment. "Bralo has provided voluntarily and without condition a factual basis for his guilty plea, the content of which greatly exceeded," I highlight that, "the original indictment against him." 54.2 of the appeal brief, I have already dealt the fact that there is ample evidence to support most of what is in the indictment and to which he pled guilty. But what is interesting is that in paragraph 63 of the appeal brief, his counsel says, "Despite the paucity of evidence disclosed by the Prosecution that would incriminate Mr. Bralo, the plea shows that Mr. Bralo chose not to accept the assessment of his counsel." And the Trial Judge, or the Trial Judges at paragraph 63, understood the significance of the plea and the weight of the evidence against him. "Furthermore, while some counts were removed from the indictment it is noteworthy that a new charge of persecution as a crime against humanity was added based partly on information supplied by Bralo." I will just finish by saying that if we are, in fact, if a Blaskic review with additional evidence process, then we would ask this Court to undertake the review itself. To determine, based on all of the evidence that was submitted at the sentencing hearing and the additional evidence, including the sentencing briefs, including the appendices to the sentencing briefs, the pictures of the victims, the statements of the victims, particularly Witness A whose heart-rendering assistance to the Prosecution will make you understand why this is a special case. There is a series of brutal, degrading conduct by Mr. Bralo that is unrelenting for the six-week period. He has pled guilty to it and he deserves to be sentenced for it. The fact that he was a changed man during that period, and perhaps for a longer period, is interesting. But gravity of the crime and his role is what he should be sentenced for in this particular case. There are mitigating circumstances; the Prosecution admitted to those mitigating circumstances. There was cooperation; the Prosecution did its best to bring it forward so that it could be properly considered. But in the end it has little weight, and a 20-year sentence is more -- is -- is -- is what Mr. Bralo deserved. A lower sentence would do an injustice to the victims. It would do an injustice to the survivors, and it would do an injustice to the Tribunal. Thank you. I'll answer any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Schomburg has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. As a matter of fact I have two questions. The first one, to keep the record straight, and let me say first of all that I am extremely grateful to you, Mr. Kremer, to highlight also the other side of the coin, so that we have the entire picture why we are sitting here today. The Defence claimed earlier on this day that there was indeed no bargaining. Comparing the 1995 indictment with the 2005 indictment, it is obvious that one count was added, namely persecution, based on the fact that the jurisprudence has developed, and the same conduct under the jurisprudence qualifies also as persecution. However, what about Counts 18 to 21 where it read in the initial indictment against Mr. Bralo that, to put it short, "Later that night, Bralo returned to the same house and had forcible oral, vaginal, and anal sex intercourse with Witness A. Bralo forced Witness A to lick his penis clean after he has raped her anally. Witness A was also physically injured that she could hardly walk the following day." Could you please tell me, why is -- are these charges, 18 to 21 of the initial indictment, no longer repeated in the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: My understanding was that Mr. Bralo would not admit to those. And a decision had to be made as to whether or not to accept the plea to what he was prepared to admit to on the factual basis, and a decision was taken on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Second, maybe even more difficult question for you. During trial Prosecution took a firm stance in requesting 25 years of imprisonment, but not only this. Prosecution was also requesting a mandatory minimum of 20 years' imprisonment, mandatory minimum based on a previous decision in the case of Dragan Nikolic. So why is it that the Prosecution did not maintain this firm position and appeal it against the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The decision as to whether or not to appeal takes into account different factors. And having regard to the reasoning of the Trial Chamber and giving deference to the discretion on sentencing, it was felt that it was not appropriate to appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We will now have another break and, when we resume, the Defence will reply. We will have a 15 to 20-minute break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I am now going to give the floor to the Defence for its reply. You have 45 minutes, that's what we provided for. If you could take less than 45 minutes, it would be agreeable to everyone. But in any case, you have 45 minutes at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Madam President, I am obliged. I hope not to take the full 45 minutes. I'm going to address just some of the points that have been raised. And I take them in no particular order. And I hope my submissions can be effectively bullet points answering simple points that have been made, much in the way of headlines. The first headline came from Ms. Carey's address to you in her confirmation that the material supplied by Mr. Bralo did confirm the Blaskic -- that General Blaskic was commander of Alpha Force. Now, that is -- in fact, on this day, the day of the Appeal Hearing, the first time that the Prosecutor has made such a clear assessment of the utility of the material supplied by Mr. Bralo. I am mindful of the question asked in your scheduling order to the Prosecution to address use and to address value, and in all of the pleadings that have gone backwards and forwards in this case, there has not been that direct and clear assessment until now. So we're grateful for that. But in our respectful submission, that is information which should have been available to the Trial Chamber and it should have been available throughout the period of this case as Rule 68 disclosure. The second headline is the test that Ms. Carey has set out to judge the utility of evidence. And Your Honours will recall criteria from that test: Is the information applicable to the Defendant or to others too? Is it information not currently in the possession of the Prosecution authority? Is it used? Well, those are criteria which, in this case, are all answered positively in favour of this Appellant; Mr. Bralo's actions pass that test. She goes on to elucidate another test, which is a test that -- as she calls it, a full and frank disclosure. Having set out that headline, she cited the English case of Crown against A and B. And as I was looking at that case, I see nothing in that case about a duty of full and frank disclosure. Indeed, quite the contrary. This is one of those English cases which concerns the Court looking at a potential informant, saying: We are grateful for your information. And the Courts view the utility in this way, not as the Prosecution have invited you to: Is the glass half empty? The English courts and other domestic courts, and, I submit, the international courts, look at the question of utility and say: Is the glass half full? What's there? What is there that we can use? If there is something there of substance, then we will recognise it. And if justice owes a debt to this informant, if the state is grateful to the supplier of this information, then the state will reflect that in passing an appropriate sentence. So I'm not aware from the submissions Your Honours have heard where any test is set out for full and frank disclosure, whether or not that -- that's a test which -- is one which is passed or failed by Mr. Bralo. We also heard from Ms. Carey about the suggestion that when those documents are supplied in the Ljubicic proceedings, they do not indicate use. Well, I quite acknowledge that it was my phraseology that may have left Your Honours thinking that a particular phrase I used might have been a play on words, and I hope I've addressed Your Honours' concerns in relation to that and you know exactly what my submissions were intended to say. But the idea that the Prosecution can serve material which they say, in inverted commas, "has the potential to aid an indication of future use," close inverted commas, and that doesn't count to use, it counts as use, is -- has to be an absurd proposition, does it not? That would mean that somebody who supplies information which is intended for future use, if that use has not yet occurred at the time of sentence, gets no credit for it. And yet, the Prosecution have it in their bank account. So it is, in my submission, a real struggle to see how those words carry their normal and natural meaning. Might have been different if that material had been served as unused material, but it was served for use, not anything else. If I might address the question of the state of knowledge of the Defence at the time the sentence hearing itself. And I'm responding in part to Your Honour Judge Shahabuddeen's question about the need for disclosure in advance of the sentence hearing and why there could not have been, as the Defence sought, such disclosure on such terms as to confidentiality, as permitted them to make informed submissions. Now, in our submission there should have been confidential disclosure in the light of what we now know, whether it was disclosure from the Trial Chamber or whether it was disclosure from the Blaskic review Chamber and, of course, it is not for the Blaskic review Chamber to act of their own initiative; it's the same Prosecution in both Chambers. And when it is apparent that Defence counsel, and indeed perhaps the Trial Chamber itself, would otherwise be deprived of the information they need to come to proper assessments of the quality of evidence, then it is an absolute duty to ensure that a miscarriage of justice does not result from their failure to seek disclosure of the material. So just recalling the sentence hearing, there had been a Rule 68 compliance notice served the day before the hearing, Your Honours will recall. And that was, as I recall, something of a shock that there was absolutely no material of any kind. What was not disclosed prior to the hearing was that the Prosecution had also supplied an ex parte filing, a document which has now been disclosed to us. So that was not disclosed to the Defence, we did not know it existed and, indeed, when one looks at the transcript of the sentence hearing one sees how that ever emerged. It was closed session towards the end of the discussion about cooperation where the fact of there having been some type of filing was blurted out by Prosecution counsel. And Your Honours will have seen those exchanges. But there is no suggestion that it was done in a formal way or in an informal way in advance of the hearing. We simply didn't know. And even having heard that there was some sort of filing, we still didn't know whether that was a filing to say the Defence think there's something, but there isn't. Or there is a proceeding but Mr. Bralo's evidence is not used. Or, as there should have been, there is a proceeding, it is used, and it is used in this particular way. There has been discussion of whether or not Mr. Bralo was bound to plead guilty to offences on the indictment. And, of course, the events of Ahmici were notorious, but in Mr. Kremer's address he has inadvertently repeated an error which has occurred, as Your Honours will know, on a number of occasions. The defendant's nickname is not "Ciko," C-i-k-o, but "Cicko," C-i-c-k-o. And it was apparent in the Blaskic proceedings, and the Kordic proceedings as well, that there were at least three persons with the names Ciko or Cicko. And indeed, the second name of Ciko appears in the factual basis as one of those who were present and active in relation to Count 1. Now, was the Defendant bound to plead guilty? Well, one can consider the original indictment and, in fact, there is a contemporaneous record of how the Prosecution viewed that back in 1997 in the Cayley document, which expressed those ex parte observations to the Blaskic Trial Chamber. When Your Honours look at the Cayley document, you'll see that there's a reference to exactly what the use is to be made of the documents supplied by Mr. Bralo. And indeed, Mr. Bralo's status there, is there expressed an intention to amend the indictment, and indeed to widen the indictment from that which had already been indicted as of 1997. Now, that amending or widening of the indictment was, in fact, never done. And when one looks at how matters came to the Trial Chamber in July of 2005, one notes that -- in terms of supporting materials, there were simply two additional statements that were supplied to the Trial Chamber. The only other supporting material was the factual basis itself. And further, those two supporting documents were disclosed for the first time to the Defence actually after - not before, but after - the hearing at which the pleas were entered. So it is not as if the Defendant was faced with an overwhelming evidential case supported by prepared materials by the Prosecutor. Indeed, our sentence brief set out as its paragraph 27 -- sorry, 27.2, an agreed formula -- set out at paragraph 27.2, an agreed formula about the status of evidence in relation to Count 1, setting out what evidence the parties agreed could have been proved to the required standard, what evidence could have -- sorry, what matters could have been demonstrated only as a prima facie case, and what evidence was dependent wholly on new information from the Defendant. The last point to make is, of course, that one is reminded that amongst the material that could be relied on is the 1997 confession by the Defendant to the UN forces, and that's material provided by him as a foundation for the count. There's further been reference to the later counts, and the reference to the relationship between the Defendant and Mr. Furundzija. Well, that is set out, and the facts of that are set out, definitively at paragraph 27 of the factual basis. The next point also concerns the factual basis. It is said by Ms. Carey that there is nothing in the factual basis that is not necessary to prove Count 1. And, with respect, we take issue with that. We've referred to five paragraphs which we say contain different information than was required in order to prove Count 1. And indeed in particular it's -- it's paragraph 7, 8, and 9, which were used in the Blaskic review proceedings, and the critical piece of information was that Ahmici was a pre-planned, surprise operation. A pre-planned, surprise operation. That information came from Mr. Bralo in the factual basis. It's not in the indictment, wouldn't have to be in the indictment, not necessary for the indictment; it's true information which was supplied by him because it is true, and it is those representations which in particular were relevant to the Blaskic review, as I understand it. Your Honours, there is a final point, which is this: The question of the Defence seeking a ruling as to whether it was cooperation or substantial cooperation, and whether it was cooperation with the Prosecution specifically or with the Tribunal with -- as Your Honours have said, its many heads. Well, firstly, as to the assessment that we were in a position to make, and, of course, everything that we said flowed from our assessment of the case ourselves. We, of course, were denied certain material about the significance of Mr. Bralo's cooperation as a result of a judicial decision. Whether that was a right or a wrong decision, nevertheless it was a judicial decision. We were denied other material by, at best, prosecutorial oversight. And, as a result, we were not in possession of the material that we should have been, and any Defence team should have been, prior to a sentence hearing. And in our submission it's wholly wrong for the Prosecution to seek to rely on their own, at best, oversight in failing to disclose in order to criticise a decision by Defence counsel which is taken, so to speak, in the dark. Your Honours, the final point that -- as I have as a bullet point, is the question of confidentiality. That's the remaining question from those that had been asked in the scheduling order. And I hope I can answer it in this way: We've attempted to tailor our submissions to ensure that it doesn't become an issue and has not become an issue in the course of this Appeal Hearing, and I hope we have achieved that. Your Honours, that's how we reply to the submissions that have been made by the Prosecution. Unless Your Honours have any questions, I wonder if now is the moment to hear from Mr. Bralo. I understand that he wishes to take your invitation to present a short speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Thank you, Mr. Cooper. We are now going to give the floor to Mr. Bralo. You have some 15 minutes to address the Chamber. THE APPELLANT BRALO: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be even briefer than that. But I do feel duty-bound to repeat before this Chamber my sincere admission of guilt and my contrition. I wish to apologise to all the victims that I might -- that my actions might have injured in any way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bralo. You may be seated. Before closing, I wish to thank all the participants in this hearing, in particular the interpreters and the court reporters. The hearing stands adjourned. You will have the decision in due course.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.32 p.m.
